expertInsight: Business Analyst surprised me with how much it leans into stakeholder management and discovery techniques over platform configuration. About a third of my exam was pure BA methodology, elicitation techniques, user story formats, acceptance criteria, and how to prioritise a backlog when stakeholders disagree. The Salesforce-specific questions focus on when to recommend declarative vs. programmatic solutions and how to translate business requirements into data model decisions. I’d recommend spending equal time on Agile/Scrum concepts as on the platform itself, the 72% passing score is one of the highest for consultant-level exams.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Business Analyst Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is a moderate exam with an unusually high pass mark. Roughly half of it is business analysis method, such as running discovery and writing user stories, and half is Salesforce knowledge, such as knowing what the platform can do before you promise it.
bullets: 72% to pass, about 44 correct answers out of 60. That is higher than most consultant exams, so there is little room for error. Confirm it in the official exam guide before you book.
Method as well as product. Elicitation techniques, process mapping and user stories carry real weight.
Salesforce judgement. You need to know when configuration will do and when something needs building.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can run a discovery session in your head: who you would talk to, which technique you would use, what you would produce, and how you would get it agreed. Aim for 80% or more on practice tests, given the 72% bar.

examFormat.heading: Business Analyst Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a moment in a project, such as stakeholders who disagree or a requirement that keeps changing, and ask what the analyst should do next.
bestWayToPass: Know which technique fits which situation: Interviews, workshops, observation, surveys and document analysis each suit different problems.
Write user stories properly: Role, goal and benefit, with acceptance criteria that can actually be tested.
Map processes before solutions: Current state first, then future state, with the gaps named.
Learn the Salesforce limits that matter: Enough to know when a requirement is cheap, expensive or impossible.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers the business analyst's work on Salesforce projects: discovering and documenting requirements, writing user stories, mapping processes, managing stakeholders and supporting testing and adoption.

keyConcepts.h2: Business Analyst: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Discovery and Elicitation
blocks.body: Requirements have to be drawn out, not collected. **Interviews** suit depth with one person and sensitive topics. **Workshops** suit getting a group to agree, and are efficient when decisions need several people in the room. **Observation**, watching someone do the job, catches the steps people forget to mention. **Surveys** reach many people for simple questions but cannot probe. **Document analysis** and reviewing the existing system show what is really happening today. Choose by what you need: depth, agreement, breadth or evidence. Prepare questions in advance, record decisions, and send back what you heard so people can correct it.

blocks.heading: User Stories and Acceptance Criteria
blocks.body: A **user story** names the role, the goal and the benefit: as a sales rep, I want to see a customer's open cases on the opportunity, so that I know about problems before a renewal call. The benefit matters because it is what gets the story prioritised or dropped. **Acceptance criteria** say how you will know it works, in terms a tester can check. Good stories are small enough to build in one iteration, independent of each other where possible, and negotiable in how they are implemented. A story that describes a screen layout rather than a need has usually jumped to a solution too early.

blocks.heading: Stakeholders and Getting Decisions Made
blocks.body: Projects stall on people, not features. Map stakeholders by how much **influence** they hold and how much **interest** they have, and plan how often to involve each group. Name a decision-maker for each area before you need one, so disagreements have somewhere to go. When stakeholders want different things. Take it back to the business goal and the evidence from discovery rather than seniority. Keep a **RAID** style record of risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, and make assumptions explicit, because an unspoken assumption is the usual cause of a late surprise.

blocks.heading: Process Mapping and Gap Analysis
blocks.body: Map the **current state** before designing anything, because the described process and the real one usually differ. Then map the **future state**, and the difference between them is your **gap analysis**, which becomes the backlog. Keep maps at a level people can read: swimlanes showing who does what are usually enough. Note where work leaves Salesforce for email or spreadsheets, since those are where errors and delays live. A map also protects you later, when someone asks why a step was removed.

blocks.heading: Requirements, Testing and Adoption
blocks.body: Separate **functional** requirements, what the system must do, from **non-functional** ones such as performance, security, accessibility and volume, which are easy to forget and expensive to retrofit. Keep **traceability** from a business need through to the story and the test, so you can show that each requirement was delivered. Plan **user acceptance testing** with real users against the acceptance criteria, not a demo given by the project team. Then plan adoption: training, communication and a measure of whether people are actually using it, because an unused solution has not solved the problem.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Business Analyst Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions ask what the analyst should do next. The right answer usually moves toward better understanding or a recorded agreement, rather than jumping to build something.

blocks.heading: Choosing an Elicitation Technique
blocks.body: Depth and sensitivity: interview. Agreement across a group: workshop. What people actually do: observation. Breadth on simple questions: survey.

blocks.heading: User Stories
blocks.body: Role, goal, benefit, plus acceptance criteria a tester can check. If it describes a screen rather than a need, it is a solution in disguise.

blocks.heading: Process Mapping
blocks.body: Current state first, then future state, then the gap. Swimlanes show who does what, and where work leaves the system.

blocks.heading: Testing
blocks.body: User acceptance testing is run by users against the acceptance criteria. A project-team demo is not UAT.

blocks.heading: Stakeholders
blocks.body: Map influence against interest, name decision-makers early, and settle disagreements with the business goal and discovery evidence.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Consultant Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after Business Analyst:

sampleQuestions.question: What is the primary focus of a Certified Business Analyst in Salesforce projects?
options: Understanding business needs, capturing requirements, and collaborating with stakeholders
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certified Business Analysts understand business needs, capture requirements, and collaborate with stakeholders to develop Salesforce solutions that drive business improvements.
whyWrong: Writing Apex code is a developer task, not the Business Analyst's core requirements-focused role.
Designing email campaigns is a Marketing function, unrelated to business analysis.
Managing server infrastructure is an IT operations task, unrelated to business analysis.

sampleQuestions.question: Which technique is commonly used to discover and document business requirements?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Stakeholder interviews and workshops are standard techniques for discovering and documenting business requirements.
whyWrong: Deployment scripts are a technical release artifact, not a requirements-discovery technique.
API development is a technical implementation task, not a requirements-discovery technique.
Unit testing is a developer QA activity, not a requirements-discovery technique.

sampleQuestions.question: What deliverable does a Business Analyst typically produce before development begins?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Business Analysts produce requirements documents and user stories to guide solution development.
whyWrong: Test classes are a developer QA artifact, not the BA's pre-development deliverable.
Integration code is a technical implementation artifact, not the BA's pre-development deliverable.
A deployed package is a technical release artifact, not the BA's pre-development deliverable.

sampleQuestions.question: How should a Business Analyst prioritize requirements when conflicts exist?
options: Align with business objectives and stakeholder agreement
sampleQuestions.explanation: Prioritization should align with business objectives and involve stakeholder agreement.
whyWrong: Deferring all decisions to IT abdicates the BA's role in facilitating stakeholder alignment.
Always choosing the technical option ignores stakeholder needs and business objectives entirely.
Choosing the cheapest option ignores business objectives and stakeholder needs, which should drive prioritization.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Salesforce artifact helps translate business requirements into implementable features?
sampleQuestions.explanation: User stories and acceptance criteria translate business requirements into clear, implementable features for the team.
whyWrong: A deployment checklist is a release-management artifact, not a requirements-translation artifact.
Process Builder is a legacy automation tool, not a requirements-translation artifact.
A debug log is a technical troubleshooting artifact, unrelated to translating requirements into features.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the standard format for writing a user story in Agile projects?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The standard user story format is "As a [role], I want [goal] so that [benefit]." This keeps focus on who needs the feature, what they need, and why, anchoring development decisions to real user outcomes.
whyWrong: '[Actor] performs [action]...' isn't the standard Agile user story format, that's 'As a [role], I want [goal] so that [benefit]'.
'Given/when/then' describes a Gherkin/BDD acceptance-criteria format, not the standard user story format itself.
'The system shall...' is a traditional requirements-statement format, not the Agile user story format.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of Acceptance Criteria in a user story?
options: To define the specific conditions that must be met for the story to be considered done by the product owner
To describe the technical implementation approach for the development team
To list the dependencies and risks associated with the user story
To document the performance benchmarks expected from the solution
sampleQuestions.explanation: Acceptance Criteria are the pass/fail conditions for a user story, they define exactly what the product owner will test to confirm the story is complete. Without clear acceptance criteria, teams risk rework due to ambiguous definitions of done.
whyWrong: Acceptance criteria don't describe technical implementation, that's a separate development concern.
Acceptance criteria aren't about listing dependencies/risks, that's separate project documentation.
Acceptance criteria aren't about performance benchmarks, that's a non-functional requirement, not what acceptance criteria define.

sampleQuestions.question: A Business Analyst is documenting the current workflow of a business process before designing a new solution. What is this activity called?
sampleQuestions.explanation: As-Is process analysis captures the current state of a business process to identify inefficiencies, pain points, and gaps before designing a To-Be (future state) solution, preventing the team from automating broken processes.
whyWrong: Solution validation confirms the built solution meets needs, it isn't the current-state documentation activity being described.
Stakeholder mapping identifies stakeholder influence, it isn't about documenting current-state workflows.
Requirements traceability links requirements to test cases, it isn't about documenting current-state workflows.

sampleQuestions.question: Which technique helps a Business Analyst understand the relative importance of stakeholders and their influence on a project?
options: Stakeholder Analysis using a Power/Interest Grid
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Power/Interest Grid plots stakeholders by their influence (power) and interest in the project, guiding the BA on how to engage each group: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, or monitor.
whyWrong: Process Decomposition breaks down processes into steps, not stakeholder influence.
Gap Analysis identifies shortfalls between current and desired state, not stakeholder influence specifically.
User Story Mapping visualizes story sequencing, not stakeholder influence specifically.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a Requirements Traceability Matrix on a Salesforce project?
options: To map database tables to Salesforce objects
To document the hierarchy of roles and permissions in the org
To track the deployment history of changes across sandbox environments
To link each business requirement to specific user stories, features, and test cases, ensuring all requirements are addressed and tested
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Traceability Matrix ensures end-to-end coverage: every business requirement maps to at least one user story, and every user story maps to test cases. It prevents requirements from being missed during development or testing.
whyWrong: A traceability matrix isn't about mapping database tables, that's a data architecture concern.
Documenting role/permission hierarchy is a security configuration concern, not what a traceability matrix does.
Tracking deployment history across sandboxes is a release-management concern, not what a traceability matrix does.

sampleQuestions.question: A project team discovers the solution being built does not address several original business requirements. Which BA technique identifies this type of shortfall?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Gap Analysis compares the current state (or planned solution) against the desired future state, identifying gaps where requirements are not addressed. It is typically performed during discovery and at key review points.
whyWrong: A Process Flow Diagram visualizes process steps, not specifically the requirement-to-solution shortfall being described.
A Risk Register tracks project risks generally, not specifically requirement-to-solution shortfalls.
A RACI Chart defines roles and responsibilities, not requirement shortfalls.

sampleQuestions.question: Which type of requirement describes system performance, security, usability, or scalability expectations rather than specific functionality?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs) define quality attributes, how the system performs rather than what it does. Examples: page load times, concurrent user capacity, data security standards. They are often overlooked but critical for solution success.
whyWrong: Functional Requirements describe specific features/functionality, not performance/security/usability characteristics.
Technical Specifications describe implementation details, not the broader quality-attribute category being asked about.
Business Requirements describe high-level business needs, not the specific technical quality attributes described.

sampleQuestions.question: During a discovery workshop, stakeholders from two business units give conflicting requirements for the same field. What is the BA's best first action?
options: Implement the version requested by the most senior stakeholder
Escalate the conflict to the project manager for resolution
Choose the simpler option to reduce implementation complexity
Document both versions and facilitate a follow-up session to align stakeholders on a single agreed requirement
sampleQuestions.explanation: Conflicting requirements should be documented and resolved through structured stakeholder facilitation, not unilaterally decided by the BA. A dedicated alignment session surfaces the business rationale behind each request and builds consensus.
whyWrong: Implementing the senior stakeholder's version without alignment risks alienating the other business unit and doesn't resolve the underlying conflict.
Escalating immediately to the project manager skips the BA's own facilitation role in resolving stakeholder conflicts.
Choosing the simpler option ignores the actual business needs driving each stakeholder's requirement.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the DACI framework define in Salesforce project governance?
options: Deployment steps across sandbox, staging, and production environments
The automation logic sequence for approval processes and flows
Decision-making roles: Driver (owns the process), Approver (final decision), Contributor (provides input), and Informed (kept updated)
The data architecture layers for custom objects, fields, and relationships
sampleQuestions.explanation: DACI (Driver, Approver, Contributor, Informed) clarifies who is responsible for driving a decision to closure, who has final approval authority, who contributes expertise, and who only needs to be informed of the outcome.
whyWrong: DACI isn't about deployment steps, that's a release-management concern, not a decision-making framework.
DACI isn't about automation logic, that's a technical implementation concern, not a governance framework.
DACI isn't about data architecture, that's an unrelated technical concept.

sampleQuestions.question: What format do user stories typically follow in Salesforce projects?
options: As a [role], I want [goal] so that [benefit]
As a [system], I want [data] so that [report]
sampleQuestions.explanation: User stories follow the format: As a [role], I want [goal] so that [benefit]. This connects the user, the capability, and the business value.
whyWrong: 'As a [user], I need [permission]...' isn't the standard user story format, the standard format centers on role/goal/benefit.
'As a [admin], I need [field]...' isn't the standard user story format, it's overly specific to one scenario.
'As a [system]...' misrepresents the format, which centers on a human role/persona, not a system.
